X, MONTH 2026 1 Spatial-Frequency Learning for Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy Image Enhancement Hesong Li, Ying Fu, Senior Member, IEEE, Ziqi Wu, Ruiwen Shao, and Tao Zhang Abstract—Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) enables the observation of atomic arrangements at sub-angstrom resolution and plays a key role in the discovery and characterization of advanced materials. Raw STEM images are often noisy and blurred due to multiple degradations. Although recent deep learning methods improve STEM images, their performance remains limited under severe degradations. In this work, we propose a spatial-frequency learning framework for STEM image enhancement. Specifically, we design a spatial-frequency fusion network that exploits periodic atomic arrangements in the frequency domain and restores local atomic details in the spatial domain. Spatial- and frequency-domain features are enhanced separately and then fused. We also present a STEM noise calibration method for synthesizing more realistic STEM images. The parameters of scan noise, pointwise noise, and background noise are estimated through statistical analysis and fitting of real STEM images. Using these calibrated parameters, we construct a diverse dataset containing a wider range of atomic arrangements, imaging modes, and degradations. Random masks combine different atomic arrangements to simulate interfaces between multiple materials. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art enhancement performance on synthetic datasets and real images of advanced materials while improving atomic localization accuracy. Index Terms—Scanning transmission electron microscopy, im- age enhancement, spatial-frequency learning, noise calibration, data generation, atomic localization. I.

INTRODUCTION Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) en- ables scientific observation at the atomic scale and plays a crucial role in the discovery and study of materials. Recent studies have discovered new properties of advanced mate- rials using STEM, including semiconductor materials [1], [2], superconducting materials [3], new energy materials [4]– [6], functional materials [7], [8], neuromorphic computing materials [9], and nanodevices [10]. Although STEM provides atomic-scale resolution, its im- ages are susceptible to multiple types of noise [11], [12]. These include scan noise caused by probe jitter, pointwise noise introduced during signal readout, and background interference Hesong Li and Ying Fu are with the School of Computer Science and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China. Our spatial-frequency fusion network (SFFN) outperforms AtomSegNet [12], FCN [13], AST [14], GAN [15], FADC [16], and SFIN [17] on three datasets (i.e., TEMImageNet [12], SFIN dataset [17], and our AtoMix). HAADF and BF denote two imaging modes, namely high-angle annular dark-field imaging and bright-field imaging, respectively. caused by impurities. These types of noise can overwhelm useful signals and hinder the observation of material structures. To avoid sample damage, both the exposure time and electron- beam intensity are constrained, further increasing the noise level. Moreover, spherical aberration blurs atomic contours and makes different atoms difficult to distinguish.

Therefore, STEM image enhancement is needed to improve the visual- ization and analysis of material structures. Simple image filtering methods (e.g., Gaussian filter, Wiener filter [18], and bilateral filter [19]) can partially remove noise, but their effectiveness is limited, and they cannot eliminate background interference and spherical aberration. Recently, some deep learning-based methods [12], [13], [15], [20] have been designed for electron microscope image enhancement. Unsupervised methods (e.g., UDVD [20]) typically utilize continuous multi-frame STEM images as training data. Since adjacent frames are used as supervision signals, they can only remove noise that varies across frames, but struggle to eliminate background and spherical aberration, which persist in every frame. By synthesizing simulated noisy images and ground truth images, supervised methods (e.g., AtomSegNet [12], FCN [13], and GAN [15]) can simultaneously remove noise, background, and spherical aberration, and generate out- put images suitable for other tasks such as atomic localization. arXiv:2610.36487v1 [cs.CV] 27 Oct 2026 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. XX, NO. X, MONTH 2026 2 Therefore, the performance of neural networks and the quality of synthetic data determine the effectiveness of the STEM image enhancement methods. One challenge is that STEM image signals are often over- whelmed by noise, making accurate feature extraction difficult. Existing networks [12], [13] mainly process spatial-domain features and neglect the strong prior induced by periodic atomic arrangements in the frequency domain. To address this issue, we design a spatial-frequency fusion network for STEM image enhancement. Our network restores atomic con- tours in the spatial domain while exploiting frequency-domain priors to suppress noise and enhance periodic structures. It processes features in both domains and adaptively fuses their complementary information. As shown in Fig.

1, our network outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The second challenge is the lack of realistic data for training deep learning models. On one hand, the prolonged exposure can damage the material sample and does not eliminate background and spherical aberration, so the ideal clean STEM images as supervised labels cannot be obtained through actual imaging. On the other hand, existing synthetic datasets [11], [12], [21] lack reality in noise distribution. STEM images have unique scan noise related to image gradients, making traditional calibration methods requiring uniform calibration frames [22], [23] unavailable. Thus, existing datasets usually use random noise parameters, which are different from those in real STEM images. In this work, we design a STEM image calibration method capable of getting various noise parameters from STEM images with atomic patterns, which does not require uniform calibration frames. We calibrate the noise parameters in real STEM images and apply them to synthesize noisy images, thereby ensuring the reality of the simulated STEM images in our dataset. Existing datasets also lack variety, and their scope of application is limited. First, they only include regular atomic patterns and exclude random arrangements, which often appear at material interfaces and are key parts in observing material changes. They also lack images with multiple arrangements. Second, they only include High-Angle Annular Dark-Field (HAADF) mode images, missing Bright-Field (BF) mode images, which are more suitable for light atoms observation [24]–[26]. Third, most datasets lack simulations of more complex degradations, including spherical aberration, lower atomic brightness, and lower resolution. To address these issues, we construct a new dataset called AtoMix, which contains images with mixed atomic arrangements. It includes simulations of the various imaging modes, atom arrangements, and degradations mentioned earlier, ensuring data diversity.

Our dataset includes complex degraded images that are closer to real-world data. Experimental results show that both our spatial-frequency fusion network and our AtoMix dataset are effective for STEM image enhancement. Our method makes STEM images clearer and atomic localization more accurate. The application results on various advanced materials demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its role in material research. This paper is an extension of a preliminary conference paper SFIN [17]. Table I summarizes the main extensions from the conference version to this journal version. In terms of network architecture, we design the Spatial-Frequency Fusion Network (SFFN), which replaces the fixed spatial-frequency addition in SFIN with learnable spatial-frequency fusion and further introduces frequency-position guidance for fine-grained frequency-domain processing.

In terms of dataset, we build AtoMix by expanding the atom patterns from 15 patterns from 5 crystal systems to 46 patterns from 7 crystal systems, in- troducing mixed atomic arrangements for simulating material interfaces, and incorporating stronger degradations, including spherical aberration, lower brightness, and lower resolution. These extensions enable our method to achieve stronger en- hancement performance on synthetic datasets and real data of advanced materials. In addition, we add comparisons with more methods, including transformers, unsupervised methods, and other frequency-domain processing networks, as well as more visual analyses of frequency-domain processing and a detailed introduction to our data synthesis method. II. RELATED WORK In this section, we provide an overview of the related work, including STEM image enhancement, frequency domain networks, and STEM image synthesis. STEM image enhancement. Natural-image enhancement and recognition [27]–[45] have been widely studied. Transformer- based methods [46]–[50] and diffusion models [51]–[53] lever- age long-range dependencies and degradation modeling to achieve superior image restoration performance. For STEM images, three commonly used traditional enhancement meth- ods are the Gaussian filter, Wiener filter [18], and bilateral filter [19], which have been integrated into electron mi- croscopy data processing software such as Gatan Microscopy IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. XX, NO. X, MONTH 2026 3 Suite. These methods can suppress noise but cannot remove background interference or spherical aberration. Recently, deep learning-based methods [12], [13], [15], [17], [54] have achieved better enhancement performance. A fully convolu- tional network [13] enhances images and identifies atomic defects, including vacancies and substitutions.

A generative adversarial network [15] is pretrained on the large-scale cell electron microscopy dataset CEM500k [55] and fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as STEM image enhancement using the TEMImageNet dataset [12]. AtomSegNet [12] is a convolutional neural network based on the U-Net architecture [56]; it is trained on TEMImageNet [12] for STEM image enhancement and atomic localization. AtomSegNet has played a key role in studies of new battery materials [4]–[6]. Several unsupervised methods (e.g., UDVD [20], 3D-B2U [57], and ZeroIG [58]) have been proposed for denoising electron mi- croscopy or natural images. Although these methods do not require synthetic training data, the absence of ideal ground- truth supervision limits their ability to remove background interference and correct atomic-contour distortions. Existing STEM image enhancement methods [12], [13], [15] operate primarily in the spatial domain and therefore fail to exploit the strong frequency-domain information inherent in periodic atomic arrangements. Frequency-domain networks. Image signals and noise typ- ically lie in different frequency ranges. Recent studies in natural image processing show that incorporating frequency- domain processing into networks helps distinguish image signals from noise and recover image details. DeepRFT [59] employs Fourier transformation for image deblurring, FSNet [60] dynamically decomposes and selects frequency-domain features, and FADC [16] and FDConv [61] use frequency analysis to guide convolutional feature processing. These existing frequency-domain methods mainly use frequency information to guide spatial-domain processing or perform frequency selection, rather than directly modeling individual frequency locations. In contrast, our SFFN directly processes features in the Fourier domain and introduces frequency- position guidance to distinguish different diffraction spots.

Existing coordinate-guided methods, such as CoordConv [62] and Coordinate Attention [63], inject spatial coordinates into spatial-domain features, whereas our SFFN embeds frequency coordinates into Fourier-domain features to distinguish diffrac- tion spots with different directions and periods. Existing meth- ods either use fixed addition for spatial-frequency interaction (SFIN [17] and DeepRFT [59]) or lack explicit cross-domain interaction (FSNet [60], FADC [16], and FDConv [61]), whereas our SFFN uses learnable spatial-frequency fusion to adaptively combine periodic frequency-domain structures with local spatial anomalies for fine-grained denoising of atomic- scale STEM images. STEM image synthesis. Due to the difficulty of obtaining ideal supervised labels in actual experiments, STEM image synthesis provides data support for deep learning-based STEM image enhancement methods [64], [65]. The abTEM code library [11] provides a noise-free STEM image rendering method that supports multiple imaging modes, but is slow and requires atomic structure files. TEMImageNet dataset [12] contains simulated STEM images in HAADF mode and label images for STEM image enhancement and atomic localization tasks. It includes several fixed shooting field angles and rota- tion angles and incorporates scan noise, pointwise noise, and background with random parameters. Cycle-GAN [21] is used to learn the mapping relationship between noiseless simulated STEM images and noisy real STEM images and generate more realistic STEM noise. This method relies entirely on reference STEM images and lacks flexibility in controlling various parameters in the data synthesis program. Existing synthetic datasets [12], [21] lack realistic STEM image noise and diverse atomic arrangement patterns, imaging modes, and image degradation types. This results in poor performance of the trained networks when applied to complex real-world data. III.

METHOD In this section, we first introduce the task formulation and our motivation. Then, we present our spatial-frequency fusion network. Finally, we introduce our STEM image data synthesis method, which includes clean image generation, noise calibration, and noise generation. A. Formulation and Motivation A STEM image with noise can be represented as the sum of a distorted clean image and various types of noise, i.e., Inoisy = SA(Iclean) + Nbackground + Nscan + Npointwise, (1) where Inoisy and Iclean denote the noisy and ideal clean images, respectively; SA(·) denotes the spherical-aberration degradation operator; and Nbackground, Nscan, and Npointwise denote background, scan, and pointwise noise, respectively. The additive formulation in Eq. (1) is grounded in the physical mechanisms of STEM imaging. Nbackground arises from sample contamination, which is independent of the atomic signal and is therefore modeled as additive noise. For Nscan, arising from probe jitter, and Npointwise, arising from the detector’s readout electronics and dark current, we retain additive formulations for computational tractability but explicitly account for their signal dependence by modeling their variances as functions of the local image gradient and pixel intensity, respectively. These heteroscedastic additive for- mulations reflect the empirical noise behavior while enabling independent calibration and stable deep learning optimization. STEM image enhancement aims to derive Iclean from Inoisy. For HAADF-mode images, the ideal image background is pure black, while the brightest atomic centers are pure white. In contrast, BF-mode images have a pure white background with the most significant atomic centers appearing as pure black. STEM image enhancement requires preserving the relative brightness and size of different atoms in an image, which enables the distinction of various elements from the image.

Guided by the challenges outlined in the Introduction, our methodology is driven by two core motivations. First, while the periodic atomic lattice yields strong frequency signatures that can be leveraged for noise suppression, aperiodic features (e.g., defects, interfaces, or ion embeddings) remain spatially IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. XX, NO. X, MONTH 2026 4 Noisy Image Denoised Image Frequency Domain Frequency Domain FFT Filter IFFT Fig. 2. Motivation of our spatial-frequency fusion network. FFT and IFFT stand for Fast Fourier Transform and Inverse Fast Fourier Transform, respec- tively. A simple filter in the frequency domain can achieve good denoising effects for STEM images. localized and cannot be fully characterized in the frequency domain alone. This necessitates a spatial-frequency fusion strategy that jointly enhances complementary information from both domains. To leverage the distinctive spot patterns of STEM images in the frequency domain, we embed coor- dinate information into the frequency-domain processing to enable fine-grained handling of information across different frequency bands. Second, robust model generalization requires training data that faithfully replicates real-world degradation characteristics. Since STEM scanning noise is intrinsically gradient-dependent, conventional flat-field calibration is inap- plicable, motivating our novel parameter extraction scheme. Furthermore, to bridge the simulation-to-experiment gap, our synthesized dataset explicitly incorporates mixed atomic ar- rangements, dual imaging modes (HAADF/BF), and complex degradations (e.g., spherical aberration and intensity loss). The detailed network architecture and data synthesis pipeline are elaborated in Sections III-B and III-C, respectively. B.

Spatial-Frequency Fusion Network As discussed in Section III-A, jointly modeling spatial- and frequency-domain information enables the network to capture both periodic atomic arrangements and local irregularities, thereby improving image enhancement. We next describe the overall network pipeline, the spatial-frequency fusion block, and the coordinate-guided frequency convolution used in each block. Overall pipeline. Our network follows the basic architecture of common image restoration networks [14], [66], [67], includ- ing two convolutions at the head and tail, and multiple blocks stacked in the middle, as shown in Fig. 3(a). First, a 3×3 convolution extracts shallow features from the single-channel input image to form a feature map with C channels. Multiple subsequent stacked spatial-frequency fusion blocks gradually enhance these features, where each block uses residual con- nections to stabilize training. Finally, a 3×3 convolution fuses the enhanced features into a single-channel output image. Spatial-frequency fusion block. As shown in Fig. 3(b), we design the spatial-frequency fusion block as the basic module of our network, which can simultaneously enhance the spatial and frequency domain information in the feature maps. First, the feature map with C channels is evenly divided into two parts along the channel dimension, each with C/2 channels. These two parts of features are then directed to two separate branches for enhancement in the spatial and frequency domains, respectively.

In the frequency domain branch, the 3×3 convolution is replaced by a specially designed coordinate-guided frequency convolution (Fig. 3(c)) that transforms features to the frequency domain for enhancement. It will be introduced later. The spatial- and frequency-domain branches process com- plementary information. Periodic atomic arrangements pro- duce strong frequency-domain signatures that can be enhanced by the frequency-domain branch. Moreover, because signal and noise occupy different frequency ranges, this branch can enhance atomic signals while suppressing noise.

The spatial- domain branch processes localized aperiodic structures that are difficult to characterize solely in the frequency domain, including material interfaces, atomic vacancies, and interca- lated ions. Fusing the outputs of the two branches enables more comprehensive feature enhancement. Unlike the fixed cross-domain addition used in SFIN [17], we adopt a convolutional operation to fuse features from the two domains. Specifically, the outputs of the spatial- and frequency-domain branches are concatenated along the channel dimension and then fused by a 3×3 convolution. Because the complementary information from the two domains does not necessarily follow an additive relationship, convo- lutional fusion provides greater flexibility. This change does not increase computational complexity or the parameter count relative to SFIN [17]. Coordinate-guided frequency convolution. We design the coordinate-guided frequency convolution to enhance features in the frequency domain. It distinguishes signal from noise by processing frequency-domain features augmented with frequency-position coordinates. STEM Image Synthesis It is difficult to obtain ideal supervising labels for image enhancement from STEM imaging. To train the network using paired data, it is necessary to first synthesize ideal clean images and then add various types of degradations to simulate real noisy STEM images. As shown in Fig. 4, our STEM image synthesis framework includes clean image generation, noise calibration, and noise generation. Clean image generation obtains ground-truth labels and clean images without noise by mixing different atomic arrangement patterns via masks. Noise generation progressively adds various noises to the clean images, where the noise parameters are derived from the noise calibration of real images. The following are the details of each step in the order of the data synthesis process. Atom pattern generation from units. Materials observed by STEM are mostly crystalline structures, whose atomic arrangements exhibit significant periodicity. Therefore, the entire image can be formed by tiling repeated pattern units. First, we generate 46 pattern units, each representing a periodic unit of a complete image, as shown on the left side of Fig. 4(a). These pattern units are rendered from 37 crystal structures viewed from four orientations. Because of crystal symmetry, some structures produce the same pattern when viewed from different orientations. Our dataset covers the seven major crystal systems defined by the International Union of Crystallography (IUCr), more than previous datasets [12], [21], thereby supporting a wider range of common material structures. Theoretically, a clean STEM image consists of numerous circular spots, each corresponding to an atomic column or a single atom and modeled using a 2D Gaussian distribution. The atomic species and column thickness determine the size and brightness of these spots. In HAADF images, atomic columns appear bright because the detector collects high-angle scattered electrons.

In BF images, atomic columns appear dark because scattering reduces the intensity collected by the bright- field detector [24]–[26]. The relative brightness and size of different atoms are fixed and can be simulated by the abTEM library [11]. Note that the abTEM library cannot be directly used to synthesize the STEM image dataset, as its physics- based rendering is slow and fails to flexibly synthesize images with different pattern combinations and various noises. In our data synthesis, abTEM is only used to obtain the arrangement structures of different pattern units, as well as the relative brightness and size parameters of atoms. These parameters are then used to render each atom with a 2D normal distribution. IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. XX, NO. After randomly selecting a pattern unit, we periodically tile it to form an image with a consistent atomic arrangement. To diversify the orientations and scales of the synthesized data, the pattern unit is randomly rotated and scaled for each image. The resulting interatomic spacing ranges from approximately 7 to 30 pixels, based on measurements of real STEM images. The pattern unit is then tiled along two lattice directions, α1 and α2, to fill the image. Different pattern units have different α1 and α2, which are not necessarily orthogonal.

By expressing the four image corners in the coordinate system defined by α1 and α2, we determine the number of repetitions required along each direction to cover the entire image. Mask-based pattern mixing. Observing the interface be- tween two atomic arrangements is important for analyzing interactions between materials and material growth. Therefore, the synthetic data should include combinations of multiple atomic arrangements with relatively random structures at their interfaces. Unlike previous datasets that simulate only one atomic arrangement per image, we use binarized Perlin noise [69] as a mask to mix two different arrangements. We first generate an image of one arrangement and replace the region where the mask equals 1 with another arrangement. The second arrangement is set to an empty arrangement with a probability of 0.1 to simulate the vacuum outside a material boundary. We then generate ground-truth and degraded images from the mixed atomic arrangements. To facilitate the adjustment of atomic brightness and size, each arrangement is represented as a list of per-atom attributes, including coordinates, brightness, and size, rather than being directly rendered as an image. To simulate atomic defects and ion intercalation, atoms are randomly removed from and added to the mixed arrangement. We approximate this process by relocating about 10% of the atoms to random positions. When generating ground-truth images for enhancement, the atomic sizes remain unchanged, while the brightness values are proportionally scaled so that the brightest atom has an intensity of 255 in HAADF mode. When generating ground truth for atomic localization, each atom is rendered as a disk with a radius of 1 pixel and an intensity of 255. When generating a degraded image, the radius of each atom is doubled to approximate spherical-aberration-induced probe broadening.

Spherical aberration in STEM originates from lens imperfections that broaden the probe and effectively widen its point spread function. Because the point spread function is commonly approximated by a 2D Gaussian distribution, increasing the Gaussian radius mimics this probe-broadening effect, which appears as blurred and enlarged atomic columns in the spatial domain. In addition, the intensity of the entire image is multiplied by a random value between 0.2 and 1 to simulate signal attenuation. Next, background, scan noise, and pointwise noise are sequentially added to the degraded image to form the final noisy image (Fig. 4(c)). The noise parameters are obtained by calibrating real images (Fig. 4(b)). Background calibration and generation. Background Nbackground comes from non-uniform sample thickness or im- purities such as carbon compounds after long-term electron beam exposure. It can be simulated using 2D Perlin noise [69]. Since the background varies smoothly at different spatial positions, for a small region in a noiseless HAADF image, the minimum pixel value of the region can represent the local background brightness, while the maximum value represents the atomic brightness. Therefore, by statistically analyzing the minimum values of different regions in real images after Gaus- sian blurring, the variation range of background brightness in the HAADF mode can be obtained. In contrast, for the BF mode, the background brightness is the maximum value of the pixels in the region. As shown in Fig. 4(b), small-sized patches (e.g., 32×32) I′ are cropped from the blurred image to calculate the maximum and minimum values Imax and Imin for each location. Then, the background brightness parameters βmin and βrange can be calculated as βmin =    min I′ Imin HAADF mode, 255 −max I′ Imax BF mode, (2) βmax =    max I′ Imin HAADF mode, 255 −min I′ Imax BF mode, (3) βrange = βmax −βmin, (4) where I′ represents a small block in the blurred image.

The final synthetic background is Nbackground = ( βmin1 + rβrangeNp HAADF mode, −βmin1 −rβrangeNp BF mode, (5) where 1 is an all-ones matrix of the same size as the image and Np is a 2D Perlin noise [69] between 0 and 1. r is a random number generated for each image between 0 and 1, which controls the intensity of the background. Scan noise calibration and generation. Scan noise Nscan is primarily due to the jitter of the scanning position. This results in the obtained pixel capturing random areas near IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. XX, NO. X, MONTH 2026 7 the ideal imaging location. When there is significant contrast variation in these areas (such as at the edge of an atom), the pixel value differences caused by the position shift become more pronounced. Therefore, the amplitude of scan noise is approximately proportional to the amplitude of the image gradient at that location. To calibrate its standard deviation σscan, it is first necessary to isolate the scan noise from the noisy STEM image. As illustrated in Fig. 4(b), each row of the original image is blurred using a one-dimensional Gaussian filter, resulting in a row-wise blurred image. In it, the pointwise noise is approximately removed by the row- wise blurring, leaving only background and scan noise. Then, the difference between the row-wise blurred image and the blurred image represents the scan noise image, as shown in Fig. 5(d). Fig. 5(e) presents the standard deviation of scan noise as a function of pixel brightness and image gradient amplitude, respectively. It can be observed that the standard deviation of scan noise is proportional to the amplitude of the image gradient. Thus, a linear fit can be applied to determine the slope and intercept of σscan related to image gradient amplitude, which can then be used to simulate the scan noise. Pointwise noise calibration and generation.

Pointwise noise Npointwise refers to noise that is independent between individual pixels, originating from the detector’s signal processing system [22], [23], such as dark current and readout noise. Related studies on the calibration of noise in natural images [22], [23] have confirmed that Tukey’s lambda distribution with a shape parameter provides a more accurate estimation of pointwise noise, i.e., Npointwise ∼TL(0, σpoint, λpoint), (6) where σpoint is the standard deviation and λpoint is the shape parameter. Pointwise noise can be obtained by calculating the difference between the original image and the row-wise blurred image, as shown in Fig. 5(b). Fig. 5(c) illustrates the variation of two parameters with pixel values. The standard deviation is proportional to the pixel value, while the shape parameter is a small positive constant number. Therefore, the slope and intercept of the standard deviation σpoint, along with the constant shape parameter λpoint, can be calculated from real images and used for the simulation of pointwise noise. Our calibration framework is mode-agnostic and applica- ble to common STEM modes (e.g., HAADF, BF). While scan noise, pointwise noise, and background share consistent physical origins across modes, the contrast inversion between HAADF (bright atoms) and BF (dark atoms) requires simple sign adjustments in parameter extraction (Eqs. (2)(3)(4)(5)). For other imaging modes, the same calibration pipeline can be directly applied by fitting mode-specific parameters from rep- resentative real images. The SNR of our synthesized AtoMix dataset ranges from −5.09 dB to 10.58 dB across BF and HAADF modes, where negative values reflect the extremely low-dose conditions targeted by our work (i.e., noise power exceeding signal power in beam-sensitive imaging), ensuring the practical relevance of our dataset for training enhancement models under real-world low-SNR STEM scenarios. EXPERIMENTS In this section, we first introduce the experimental setup. Then, we compare the enhancement results of different meth- ods. Finally, we analyze in detail the effectiveness of the proposed spatial-frequency learning and our AtoMix dataset. A. Experimental Settings We first provide the datasets and metrics. Then, we intro- duce the comparison methods. Finally, we provide implemen- tation details of our spatial-frequency fusion network. Datasets and metrics. We validate the effectiveness of our method on both synthetic datasets and real-world data. The synthetic datasets include TEMImageNet [12], SFIN dataset [17], and our AtoMix. The real-world data comprises pub- licly available images of four types of advanced materials (i.e., superconducting material [3], all-solid-state battery [4], nanodevice [10], and neuromorphic computing material [9]), as well as STEM images of high-entropy alloys captured in our laboratory. Following SFIN [17], we use Peak Signal-to- Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [70] to evaluate enhancement performance. Comparison methods. Our Spatial-Frequency Fusion Net- work (SFFN) is compared with two traditional methods (i.e., Gaussian filter and Wiener filter [18]), ten supervised deep learning methods (i.e., AtomSegNet [12], FCN [13], Restormer [66], SwinIR [67], AST [14], GAN [15], FS- Net [60], FADC [16], FDConv [61], SFIN [17]), and two unsupervised deep learning methods (i.e., UDVD [20] and ZeroIG [58]). AtomSegNet, FCN, Restormer, SwinIR, AST, and GAN are spatial domain networks, while FSNet, FADC, FDConv, SFIN, and our SFFN are spatial and frequency domain networks. Due to the requirement for multi-frame input images, UDVD and ZeroIG are only compared on the multi-frame real-world data captured in our laboratory. Implementation details of our network. Our SFFN is trained on AtoMix for 500 epochs using the Adam optimizer [71] (β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999) and an L1 loss.

For each of the HAADF and BF imaging modes, AtoMix contains 1,000 groups of training images and 100 groups of test images. More data can be easily synthesized if needed. The code is implemented in PyTorch [68]. The initial learning rate is set to 2 × 10−4 and reduced by half at epochs 250, 400, 450, and 475, following SFIN [17]. The mini-batch size is set to 8, allowing training to be completed on a single NVIDIA 3090 GPU. B. Discussion We first discuss the individual effectiveness of the core components of our SFFN, including coordinate-guided fre- quency convolution, frequency-coordinate embedding, and cross-domain feature fusion. Then, we discuss the effective- ness of our AtoMix dataset. Effectiveness of our coordinate-guided frequency convo- lution. We use coordinate-guided frequency convolution in each spatial-frequency fusion block to extract and enhance frequency-domain features. We first visualize its effect on enhancing periodic features and then compare it with other frequency-domain networks or modules. Input DeepRFT FSNet FADC FDConv SFIN SFFN (Ours) GT Fig. 10. Comparison of frequency processing networks on AtoMix dataset. Fig. 9 visualizes the enhancement effect of our coordinate- guided frequency convolution on the periodic information in STEM images. Fig. 9(b) shows the feature map before enhancement, where the image signals are masked by noise, making it impossible to distinguish different atoms. After enhancement, each feature map in Fig. 9(d) exhibits the same periodic variation as the real atomic arrangement in Fig. 9(c). It indicates that our coordinate-guided frequency convolution can enhance the periodic information of atomic arrangements in the image, thereby helping to recover the atomic contours from the noise. Furthermore, the features in Fig. 9(d) exhibit richer colors (such as blue and green) compared to those in Fig. 9(b). This indicates that the values of the features have been equalized to distinguish different parts of each atom. Although Fig. 9(d) exhibits clearer atomic periodicity, periodic responses also appear in the background regions.

This indicates that frequency-domain processing alone cannot distinguish different spatial locations, motivating the fusion of frequency-domain and spatial-domain features. Table III shows that, compared with the spatial-only variant SFFN- V1, introducing the coordinate-guided frequency branch in SFFN-V3 increases the PSNR from 27.80 dB to 31.60 dB, demonstrating the benefit of frequency-domain processing. Table IV compares our coordinate-guided frequency convo- lution with other state-of-the-art frequency-domain networks or modules, including DeepRFT [59], FSNet [60], FADC [16], and FDConv [61]. Although these methods incorporate frequency-domain analysis, they fundamentally differ from our approach in three key aspects. First, instead of using frequency analysis merely to guide spatial convolutions (e.g., FADC) or performing coarse frequency selection (e.g., FSNet and FDConv), our method explicitly transforms features into the IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE, VOL. This enables fine-grained modeling of distinct frequency locations, which is crucial for separating and en- hancing individual diffraction spots in STEM images. Second, we introduce explicit frequency-position guidance by append- ing the x/y coordinates of the frequency map to the frequency- domain features.

This makes the network explicitly aware of the positional context of each frequency component, enhancing its sensitivity to diffraction spot locations and thereby improv- ing atomic structure recovery under heavy noise. Third, for explicit spatial-frequency feature fusion, rather than omitting cross-domain interaction (e.g., FSNet, FADC, FDConv) or re- lying on simple addition (e.g., SFIN and DeepRFT), we design parallel spatial and frequency branches fused via concatenation followed by a convolution. This learnable fusion provides greater flexibility than fixed addition and enables the network to combine complementary spatial- and frequency-domain information based on the input features. Consequently, the model can jointly leverage periodic structural priors from the frequency domain and local spatial anomalies, such as atomic vacancies, material interfaces, and embedded ions. As shown in Table IV, our SFFN achieves higher enhancement accuracy with only 0.9M parameters while maintaining computational complexity comparable to existing methods. The contri- bution of the y coordinate is slightly larger than that of the x coordinate because the height of the frequency-domain feature map is approximately twice its width (Fig. 3(c)), allowing the y coordinate to encode more detailed positional information.
